newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic counts on protest fatigue, diversions.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic counts on protest fatigue, diversions.

text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic's strategy for mastering his worst crisis is falling into place - let Serbian protesters shout themselves into exhaustion and divert attention with cautious economic reform, analysts say.

The authoritarian leader has stayed true to form during Serbia's 10-week-old wave of unrest over annulled elections, sanctioning a few concessions of little consequence when pushed, while cultivating confusion about his end game.

Milosevic, reclusive and inscrutable as ever, has still not addressed the crux of the crisis in public -- his rival parties' claim to have won most of Serbia's biggest cities in municipal elections in November nullified by his Socialist Party (SPS).

OSCE investigators invited in by Milosevic to buy time wound up intensifying pressure on him by declaring the annulment fraudulent and confirming that the SPS had lost 14 of 18 municipalities, including Belgrade.
Milosevic muddied the waters by having the SPS concede four towns after face-saving inquiries, appeal against the Belgrade results to the Supreme Court and say nothing about the rest.

The expulsions of both a senior hardliner and a prominent moderate from the SPS -- for blatant vote fraud and opposition sympathies respectively -- have thickened the ambiguity shrouding Milosevic's intentions, analysts said.
But his reluctance to either drive protesters off the streets with brute police force or admit electoral defeat across the board now seems to be crystallising into policy.

"Milosevic has decided against drastic steps to deal with the post-election crisis, hoping he will get more room for manoeuvre in time and that external pressure will abate," the well-informed independent VIP newsletter said on Monday.

"He also expects the Serbian opposition will get tired and become disunited. In this way Milosevic hopes to consolidate his position and postpone final solutions until this autumn when the consequences (of protests) become clear."

VIP said Milosevic's strategy could well bear fruit, barring unforeseeable incidents in the streets that could spiral into open civil conflict and renewed, punitive isolation of Serbian-led Yugoslavia by the West.

But after two orchestrated attacks by pro-SPS gangs that failed to intimidate opposition protesters, the government has allowed daily demonstrations to settle into a routine which, if managed right, leave the political equilibrium unchanged.
Protesters are allowed to speechify and whistle to their hearts' content as long as they do not block traffic. To ensure that, police maintain cordons on nearby main streets.
Opposition leaders would like to turn up the heat on Milosevic with blockades but fear handing him a pretext to declare a state of emergency and ban any street dissent.

They also know the impact of Western pressure on Milosevic is limited and could backfire. There may be little more the West can do to ostracise Yugoslavia, still isolated despite the lifting of a U.N. trade embargo last year.

No major commercial and diplomatic ties have been restored and to reimpose full sanctions would hurt the poor majority of Serbs, not the SPS-sheltered power elite who black-marketeered their way to riches under the embargo, diplomats say.
And to re-quarantine Yugoslavia could play into the hands of neo-communist state propagandists who claim protesters are dupes of Western powers out to destabilise Yugoslavia.
In the meantime, Milosevic hopes to defuse pressure with government reshuffles and some reforms to revive an economy wrecked by sanctions and corruption, political sources said.

VIP said the government would soon move to privatise property, especially in service industries to help overcome a dire shortage of money for salaries of state employees, such as policemen and soldiers.
This would avoid the need to print money without backup assets and rekindle the kind of hyper-inflation that pauperised millions during the sanctions period.

Parliamentary and presidential elections are due by the end of 1997. But political sources say SPS hardliners are counting on Zajedno's popular appeal fading once they take over a few local administrations bereft of money for improvement.

However, most analysts say the protest campaign has irretrievably punctured the Socialists' image of omnipotence and that they will have to be more responsive to needs for political and economic reforms from now on.
